idiom_name: throwing initializer init(customer:lines:) throws (or a static make(from:) when the input must be transformed)
implementation_notes: Swift initializers can fail, so the factory's promise is expressed in the type system: declare init(...) throws for domain-rule failures or init? when absence is the natural outcome, and the compiler forces every caller to handle it; structs keep this clean because a failure can occur before all properties are set. What replaces the classic factory class is the throwing initializer itself; use a static factory method when inputs must first be decoded or transformed, and a standalone factory type only when creation has to call repositories, since initializers cannot be async.
pitfalls: init? loses the failure reason and forces unwrapping; prefer a throwing initializer when the rule matters and reserve init? for presence checks.
Declaring a custom initializer removes the synthesized memberwise initializer, so internal code and tests lose the raw construction path - usually the point, but it breaks fixtures that relied on it.

Class initializers have delegation rules and a partial-initialization history (failing before super.init was once a compile error); modelling aggregates as structs or using a static factory avoids those edge cases.
